title: Fourier and Complex Analysis
body:
MATH 4199 is built on one claim: a function can be written as a sum of simple waves, and
writing it that way converts hard operations into easy ones. Differentiation becomes
multiplication, convolution becomes multiplication, and a differential equation becomes an
algebraic equation. Changing the representation changes what is difficult, which is the same
move [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] makes when it changes basis, carried out in a space of functions.

The material begins with periodic functions on an interval in [[Fourier Series]], lets the
interval grow to the whole line in [[Fourier Transform]], discretises so a computer can run it
in [[Discrete Fourier Transform]], and makes that computation fast in
[[Fast Fourier Transform]]. The second half is complex analysis proper, covering integration
along contours, the [[Residue Theorem]], and a final project on the [[Mandelbrot Set]].

This is a directed readings course and it draws on more of the MATH block than any other.
[[CALCULUS 2]] supplies the integrals and the series expansion idea, [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] and
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] supply the projection-onto-a-basis argument, and
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] supplies the PDEs that are the physical reason the series exists.

## Topics

### Fourier series

A [[Periodic Function]] repeats with some fundamental period, and [[Fourier Series]] writes it
as a sum of sines and cosines whose frequencies are whole multiples of the fundamental:

$$
f(x) \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx\right)
$$

Each term is a pure tone, and the coefficients say how much of each tone the function
contains. A square wave, which has a corner and a jump, is built entirely out of smooth curves
by this expansion, using only odd harmonics with amplitudes falling as $1/n$.

[[Fourier Coefficients]] are computed by integration:

$$
a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,dx, \qquad
b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx
$$

The constant term $\frac{a_0}{2}$ is the average value of the function, an even function has
no $b_n$ terms, and an odd function has no $a_n$ terms, so checking symmetry first halves the
work.

[[Orthogonal Functions]] explains why those integrals isolate one frequency at a time:

$$
\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(nx)\cos(mx)\,dx = 0 \quad\text{whenever } n \neq m
$$

Multiplying $f$ by $\cos(nx)$ and integrating kills every term except the $n$th, which is
exactly how a coordinate is extracted in an orthonormal basis. A Fourier coefficient is a
[[Projection]] onto a basis function, and it is the [[Dot Product]] of [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] with
the sum replaced by an integral. That analogy is the organising idea of the whole first half.

[[Complex Exponential]] rewrites the expansion in terms of $e^{inx}$ through Euler's formula,
collapsing the two coefficient families into a single family $c_n$ and halving the algebra.

[[Fourier Series]] and [[Taylor Series]] both write a function as an infinite sum, and they
differ in what they are good for. Taylor uses powers of $(x-a)$ and describes behaviour near
one point, so it degrades as you move away. Fourier uses sinusoids and describes an entire
interval at once, which is what makes it the right tool for a signal.

### What the series does at the awkward points

At a jump discontinuity the series converges to the midpoint of the two one-sided limits,
which is the best any continuous partial sum can do, since no sum of continuous functions
reproduces a jump. Near the jump the partial sums overshoot by roughly 9% of the jump height, and adding
terms narrows the overshoot without reducing it. That is the [[Gibbs Phenomenon]], and it is
visible as ringing at sharp edges in a compressed image.

[[Parseval's Identity]] states that the energy is preserved:

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 = \sum|c_n|^2
$$

The total energy in the time domain equals the total in the frequency domain, which is
Pythagoras on an [[Orthonormal Basis]] with infinitely many axes. It is why discarding small
coefficients discards a known and bounded amount of the signal, which is the entire
justification for lossy compression.

### The transform

[[Fourier Transform]] takes the period to infinity, so the discrete list of frequencies becomes
a continuous spectrum and a non-repeating signal gets an expansion too. The properties table
covers linearity, time shifting, modulation and scaling, and the derivative property is what
makes the transform worth building for differential equations:

$$
\widehat{f'}(\xi) = 2\pi i \xi \,\hat{f}(\xi)
$$

Differentiation in one domain is multiplication in the other, so a differential equation
becomes algebra, gets solved, and gets transformed back.

Scaling produces a reciprocal relationship between the domains: compressing a signal in time
spreads it in frequency. A [[Dirac Delta Function]], an infinitely short pulse, contains every
frequency in equal measure, and a pure sine occupies a single frequency and lasts forever.
Nothing can be narrow in both domains at once, which is the mathematical content of the
uncertainty principle.

[[Convolution Theorem]] is the result that makes the transform indispensable:

$$
\widehat{f * g} = \hat{f}\cdot\hat{g}
$$

Convolution in one domain is pointwise multiplication in the other, so an operation costing
$O(N^2)$ directly becomes $O(N)$ after transforming. That single identity is why filtering,
polynomial multiplication and [[Image Processing]] kernels all route through the transform.

### Sampling

[[Dirac Delta Function]] is the idealised impulse, and a train of them at regular intervals is
the mathematical model of sampling, which is what an analog to digital converter performs.

[[Sampling Theorem]], due to Nyquist and Shannon, states that a signal containing no frequency
above $f_{max}$ can be reconstructed exactly from samples taken faster than $2f_{max}$. Exactly
means with no error at all, which is the claim that makes digital audio possible:

```
human hearing tops out near 20 kHz
CD audio samples at 44.1 kHz  >  2 × 20 kHz
so the continuous waveform is recoverable in full from the stored numbers
```

[[Aliasing]] is what undersampling produces. A frequency above half the sampling rate folds
down and reappears as a lower frequency that was never present, and the two are
mathematically indistinguishable in the sampled data, which is why the damage cannot be
repaired afterwards. Anti-aliasing filtering therefore has to happen before the sampler, in
analog hardware. The same effect makes a wagon wheel appear to spin backwards on film.

### The discrete transform

[[Discrete Fourier Transform]] replaces the integral with a sum over $N$ samples:

$$
X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n e^{-2\pi i k n/N}
$$

$N$ numbers in and $N$ numbers out, which is [[Matrix Multiplication]] by the DFT matrix:

```
x = [1, 1, 1, 1]     ->   X = [4, 0, 0, 0]     constant signal, all energy at frequency 0
x = [1, -1, 1, -1]   ->   X = [0, 0, 4, 0]     alternating, all energy at the top frequency
x = [1, 0, 0, 0]     ->   X = [1, 1, 1, 1]     an impulse, energy spread evenly
```

The third line is the time-frequency reciprocity above, visible in four numbers. The rows of
the DFT matrix are orthogonal, so the inverse transform is its conjugate transpose, which
means transforming back costs the same as transforming forward.

[[Roots of Unity]] are the entries of that matrix and form a [[Cyclic Group]], one of the few
places [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] pays off visibly elsewhere in the degree.
[[Fast Fourier Transform]] exploits the periodicity of those roots. Splitting the sum into even
and odd indices gives two half-size DFTs plus a linear combining pass, which is the recurrence
$T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N)$ that also produces [[Merge Sort]]:

```
N = 1024:   naive DFT   N²      = 1,048,576 operations
            FFT         N log N =    10,240 operations
            a factor of 100, and the gap widens with N
```

Convolution through the FFT beats direct convolution for the same reason: transform both
inputs, multiply pointwise, transform back.

### Complex analysis

[[Complex Convergence]] covers sequences, series and the disc of convergence, and it answers a
question [[CALCULUS 2]] leaves open. The real function $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is smooth everywhere
on the real line, and its Taylor series at 0 diverges for $|x| > 1$ with nothing on the real
line to explain why. In the complex plane the reason is visible: the function has poles at
$\pm i$, at distance 1 from the origin, and the radius of convergence is the distance to the
nearest singularity anywhere in the plane.

[[Complex Integration]] integrates along a contour and is structurally the [[Line Integral]] of
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]. Cauchy's theorem gives $\oint_\gamma f\,dz = 0$ when $f$ is analytic
inside and on $\gamma$, so all the value of a contour integral sits at the singularities. The
mechanism is one computation:

$$
\oint_{|z|=r} \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i, \qquad
\oint_{|z|=r} z^n\,dz = 0 \;\text{ for every other integer } n
$$

Only the $(z-z_0)^{-1}$ term survives, which is why the residue is defined as that
coefficient. [[Residue Theorem]] collects it:

$$
\oint_\gamma f\,dz = 2\pi i\sum_k \operatorname{Res}(f, z_k), \qquad
\operatorname{Res} = \lim_{z\to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z) \text{ at a simple pole}
$$

The payoff is that real integrals with no elementary antiderivative become finite sums of
residues, computed by closing the contour in the complex plane and reading off the poles
enclosed.

### The final project

The [[Mandelbrot Set]] is the set of complex $c$ for which the iteration
$z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c$, started at $z_0 = 0$, stays bounded. The escape criterion is exact: any
orbit reaching $|z| > 2$ diverges, and that is provable.

```
c = -1:   0, -1, 0, -1, 0, ...        bounded, so c is in the set
c =  1:   0, 1, 2, 5, 26, ...         escaped at step 3, so c is outside
```

Escaping is therefore provable in finite time, and remaining bounded is established by no
finite computation. Every rendered image colours a point by how many iterations it survived,
and the black region is the set of points that survived an arbitrary iteration limit. The set
is recognisable and undecided, which is exactly the distinction [[Undecidability]] draws in
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].

[[Julia Set]] runs the same iteration with the roles of $z_0$ and $c$ exchanged, and $c$ lies
in the Mandelbrot set exactly when the Julia set for that $c$ is connected, so the Mandelbrot
set is an index of which Julia sets hold together.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 2]] (MATH 2200) supplies both halves of the toolkit.
  [[Trigonometric Integrals]] and [[Integration By Parts]] evaluate the coefficient integrals,
  [[Infinite Series]] and [[Convergence Tests]] decide whether the expansion converges, and
  [[Taylor Series]] and [[Maclaurin Series]] are the same move in a different basis.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) supplies [[Complex Numbers]] and [[Polar Form]], where the
  [[Roots of Unity]] come from, along with the [[Vector Space]], [[Basis]] and [[Dot Product]]
  vocabulary that [[Orthogonal Functions]] extends to infinitely many dimensions.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) is the finite-dimensional rehearsal, where
  [[Inner Product]], [[Orthonormal Basis]] and [[Projection]] are [[Fourier Coefficients]]
  with the integral replaced by a sum. It keeps [[Wavelet Transform]] and
  [[Image Processing]].
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200) is the physical reason the series exists. Separation of
  variables on the [[Heat Equation]] or the [[Wave Equation]] produces a family of modes, and
  fitting an initial condition to them is a Fourier expansion. [[Line Integral]],
  [[Parameterization]] and [[Green's Theorem]] are the real-variable rehearsal for
  [[Complex Integration]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) built the hardware this course explains. An
  [[DAC's and ADC's|ADC]] samples the waveform at the rate [[Sampling Theorem]] requires,
  [[Fidelity]] degrades at a low [[Sample Rate]] through [[Aliasing]], and [[PCM]] stores an
  [[Amplitude]] per sample, which the Dirac comb idealises.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] takes the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] as a divide-and-conquer
  algorithm alongside [[Merge Sort]], stated in [[Time Complexity]] and
  [[Asymptotic Analysis]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) is where the [[Mandelbrot Set]] lands, since
  the escape-time algorithm is a semi-decision procedure and the simple-rule-to-complex-output
  behaviour is what [[Cellular Automata]] demonstrates.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) supplies the [[Cyclic Group]] structure of the
  [[Roots of Unity]] that the DFT matrix is built from.
- [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) meets this course inside Shor's algorithm, where the quantum
  Fourier transform performs period finding and breaks RSA.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and the [[Convolutional Neural Network]] are named for the operation
  [[Convolution Theorem]] defines. The kernels are learned there and designed here, and the
  frequency-domain view is what makes fast filtering possible.
- [[THE UNIVERSE AT LARGE]] (ASTR 1103) reads a star's composition off its [[Spectra]], which
  is this course's decomposition by frequency performed on starlight.

### 2.3 Fourier Series over Other Intervals

Our goal is to generalize a [[Fourier Series]] over an interval other than $[0,2\pi]$
We can do this by introducing a function $g(t)$ Where $t$ is defined by 
$$
\begin{matrix} \\
x \in [0, 2\pi]  \\
t \in [0, L]
\end{matrix}
$$
Where
$$
x = \frac{2\pi t}{L}
$$
The above [[Linear Transformation]] provides the following mappings
$$
\begin{align*}
t = 0 &\mapsto x = 0 \\
t = L &\mapsto x = 2\pi \\
\end{align*}
$$
Then we define $g(t) = f(x(t))$ such that 
$$
\begin{align*}
f(x) &\sim \frac{a_{0}}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_{n}\cos\left(nx\right)+ b_{n}\sin\left(nx\right)\right] \\
\implies f(x(t)) = g(t) &\sim \frac{a_{0}}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_{n}\cos\left(\frac{2n\pi t}{L}\right)+ b_{n}\sin\left(\frac{2n\pi t}{L}\right)\right] \\

\end{align*} 
$$
Now we have the series expansion for $g(t)$ over $t \in [0,L]$, now we need to find the [[Fourier Coefficients]]. 

Recall that 

$$
\begin{align*}
a_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\cos(nx)dx \\
b_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)dx
\end{align*}
$$
So we can use our substitution 
$$
\begin{align*}
x=\frac{2\pi t}{L} &\implies \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{2\pi}{L} \\
&\implies dx = \frac{2\pi}{L}dt
\end{align*}
$$
Then we can find our coefficients by changing the bounds of integration and completing the substitution

$$
\begin{align*}
a_{n} &= \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{t=0}^{t=L}g(t)\cos\left(n\left(\frac{2\pi t}{L}\right)\right)\left(\frac{2\pi}{L}dt\right) \\
&= \frac{2\pi}{\pi L} \int_{t=0}^{t=L}g(t)\cos\left(\frac{2\pi nt}{L}\right)dt 
\end{align*}
$$
Likewise the $b_n$ coefficient can be found 
$$
b_{n}= \frac{2}{L} \int_{t=0}^{t=L}g(t)\sin\left(\frac{2\pi nt}{L}\right)dt
$$
